schools.summary: Henry reads the title as the key to the psalm — David fleeing Absalom (2 Sam. 15), weeping barefoot over Olivet yet composing a comfortable psalm, his flight not cowardice but the fortitude of faith, and the trouble the sword God threatened over his house for Uriah's sake; Spurgeon marks that troubles come in flocks, 'sorrow hath a numerous family.'

Gill hears David amazed that his own son and long-ruled subjects should rise against him; Calvin holds the Absalom occasion from the psalm's tenor while dismissing the titles as 'destitute of authority,' and finds David's faith in daring to pour his complaint into God's bosom.

Keil and Delitzsch title it a morning hymn of one in distress but confident in God, sharing the 'holy hill' with Psalm 2 and no evening hymn; Ellicott fills in the history — Ahithophel's twelve thousand and Hushai's flattering muster of all Israel from Dan to Beersheba.

Clarke reads the private sins of Bathsheba and Uriah publicly avenged in the revolt, Nathan's 'sword shall not depart from thy house' fulfilled, and takes the inscription as proof the psalms are not chronological.
Augustine reads the whole psalm in the Person of Christ, the undutiful son Absalom standing for the traitor Judas, from whose mind the Son of God withdrew so that the devil entered his heart.

debates.question: Do the psalm's titles carry authority as the key to its occasion?

sides.position: the inscription is the authoritative key to the occasion and the psalm's sense
the titles are mere later Jewish glosses, destitute of authority, though the Absalom occasion stands on the psalm's own tenor

outliers.note: Reads the whole psalm christologically in the Person of Christ, identifying the rebel son Absalom with the traitor Judas and 'Absalom' as meaning 'a father's peace.'

schools.summary: Gill: the taunt is spoken 'to my soul,' cutting like a sword; Calvin: the enemies' boldness grew from their confidence that God had cast David off, Absalom trusting his own power and disregarding God.

Henry unfolds the malice threefold — a spiteful construction on his troubles, a blasphemy against God's power, an attempt to drive him to despair — met by David spreading the taunt before God as Hezekiah spread Rabshakeh's letter (Ps. 35:3).

Wesley takes Selah for a musical note bidding the singer lift the voice, pause, or lengthen the tune, yet set at remarkable passages to quicken attention; Clarke weighs the derivations and leans to Selah as a nota bene, 'attend to this' (cf. higgaion, Ps. 9:16).
Ellicott calls Selah the despair of scholars — seventy-one occurrences, no ethical sense, and no strophe-marking function — and concludes it a musical term, probably a direction to play loud.

sides.position: a bare musical rubric — a pause, a lifting of the voice, or a direction to play loud
a call to the mind — a nota bene, 'mark this and consider'

themes: no help for him in God

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch render 'a shield behind me,' covering him behind and before, from the fountain-head of Gen. 15:1, and hear the paradox — the kingdom lost, yet Jahve his glory and the lifter of his head as he climbs Olivet (2 Sam. 15:30); Ellicott presses 'behind me' against Absalom's pursuers and echoes Horace.

Henry gathers the three things God is to his people — safety (a shield about them), honour (their glory though the crown fall, Isa. 60:19), and joy (the head lifted out of and under trouble); Spurgeon names the trio 'defence for the defenceless, glory for the despised, joy for the comfortless.'

Clarke reads 'the lifter up of mine head' prophetically, a settled knowledge that God would restore him; Wesley: 'my glory' the occasion of glorying in God's favour, the lifting a restoration to former dignity.
Gill hears the soldier's language — a shield about him — the same defence faith holds up in Christ's blood and righteousness against law, conscience, and Satan.

debates.question: Does the shield stand 'behind' David or 'round about' him?

sides.position: 'behind me' — a guard against the pursuers on his track
'about me,' round about — protection on every side

themes: the lifter up of the head

schools.summary: Gill takes the crying for vocal, fervent prayer (Targum 'I prayed'), loud with the ardour and importunity of a man in earnest.

Henry: care and grief do us good when they set us praying; the answer comes from the holy hill because God is not tied to the ark Zadok carried back (2 Sam. 15:25), and Christ is set King on Zion (Ps. 2:6).
Keil and Delitzsch take the hill for Zion and the verse for a retrospect on the past night's safety; Ellicott notes 'with my voice' means aloud, the present verbs marking the psalmist's habit.
Wesley reads 'his holy hill' as heaven itself (cf. Ps. 15:1); Clarke draws encouragement from the answered cry and the Selah — God never shuts out the prayer of the distressed.

debates.question: What is the 'holy hill' from which God answered?

sides.position: the earthly Zion, the ark on Mount Zion

themes: the answer from the holy hill

schools.summary: Henry opens the verse three ways — the common mercy of every night (many sleep and never wake, like Egypt's firstborn), the singular calm of David's spirit under his son's treachery, and, with the ancients, the resurrection of Christ who awaked because the Lord sustained him; Spurgeon: faith let David sleep surrounded by foes, a higher work than manly courage.

Wesley: he slept securely, casting all his cares on God; Clarke marvels at the waking, for David might humanly have been murdered in his bed by servants his son had corrupted, yet God his shield preserved him whole.
Gill weighs the sleep of grief (Jarchi — as Elijah and Jonah) against the serenity of a mind at peace, and prefers the latter, a blessing of life from the Lord.
Keil and Delitzsch fix the Hebrew as a backward glance ('and thus I fell asleep') and ground the waking in Jahve's support, God's hand the pillow.

debates.question: Whence the sleep — from grief or from faith?

sides.position: the heavy slumber that grief can bring
the serene rest of a heart stayed on God

themes: lying down and sleeping in peace

schools.summary: Henry marks the change faith has wrought — David, who sent back the ark speaking doubtfully ('let him do to me what seemeth good,' 2 Sam. 15:26), now speaks as a strong believer without fear; a cheerful resignation to God is the way to confidence in God; Spurgeon guards the courage from bravado — he does not underestimate his cunning foes yet trembles not.
Gill recalls David's lifelong courage — the lion, the bear, and Goliath — so that thousands in arms, his own son at their head, did not dismay him.
Clarke: strength and numbers are nothing against God's omnipotence; he who makes God his refuge has no cause to fear.
Ellicott glosses 'set themselves' as arrayed for battle (1 Kings 20:12); Keil and Delitzsch carry the fearlessness into the prayer 'Arise, O LORD' that follows.

themes: courage from faith not the sword
the contrast with David's earlier doubt

schools.summary: Clarke: continued protection hangs on continual prayer — 'God never ceases to help as long as we pray' — and reads 'thou hast smitten' as a confident 'thou wilt smite'; Wesley takes the smitten cheek-bone for contempt and the broken teeth for shattered strength, the foes like beasts of prey.

Keil and Delitzsch mark the bold 'Arise' taken from Moses (Num. 10:35), God arising to take a decisive part; Ellicott renders the perfects as presents ('thou smitest... breakest') and conceives the enemies as wild beasts God renders harmless.

Henry reads 'thou hast smitten' as past deliverances — God had broken Saul and the Philistines upon the cheek-bone before; Spurgeon: God has broken the teeth of the ungodly, so their toothless jaws cannot devour — 'a dragon whose head is broken.'
Gill: God can seem asleep till his people cry 'Arise' (cf. Num. 10:35); David neglects not prayer but pleads his covenant interest, addressing God as his own.

debates.question: Is 'thou hast smitten... broken' a recollection of past deliverances or a confident present/future?

sides.position: past mercies recalled — God has broken the enemy before (Saul, the Philistines)
a confident present or future seized by faith — 'thou smitest' / 'thou wilt smite'

themes: 'Arise, O LORD' — the cry for rescue

schools.summary: Henry hears faith grown triumphant, resting on two truths — that salvation is the Lord's prerogative, so all who have him for God are sure of it, and that his blessing rests surely on his people; Spurgeon calls the first clause 'the sum and substance of Calvinistic doctrine,' grace from first to last, the blessing special to God's chosen.
Gill unfolds salvation as the whole Trinity's work — resolved by the Father, wrought by the Son, applied by the Spirit.

Clarke: God alone saves and keeps his people saved; the closing Selah a double nota bene — salvation comes from God and is continued by God — the psalm falling into complaint, confidence, and petition, the king praying even for his rebel subjects.

Ellicott parts from the rest — 'let thy blessing be upon thy people' is not a statement of fact but an intercessory prayer, the mark of the true Shepherd; Keil and Delitzsch let salvation stand as the Lord's and the blessing his people's.

debates.question: Is 'thy blessing is upon thy people' a statement of fact or an intercessory prayer?

sides.position: a fact pronounced — the blessing already rests on God's people
an optative petition — 'let thy blessing be upon thy people'
